source.title: Disentangling Polysemantic Neurons with a Null-Calibrated Polysemanticity Index and Causal Patch Interventions

page_placements.theme: Apparent polysemanticity often reflects one coherent shared or related feature

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies polysemanticity in ResNet-50, but it does not test any listed version: it does not measure the Qwen3-32B audit shares, other language-model shares, the InceptionV1 examples or estimates, attribution graphs, or explanation-prediction scores.
record.gate_note: The paper reports PSI-based findings and patch-swap outcomes on ResNet-50. These are relevant to polysemanticity generally, but do not measure the specific outcome named by any claim version. The paper also reports rank stability across patch-count settings, alternative text-encoder correlation, and cluster-count distributions; these are method-sensitivity results, not measurements of the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: This study builds a polysemanticity score (PSI) for ResNet-50 channels and validates it against nulls and with patch swaps. It reports no share of neurons with one, two or unexplained jobs. It covers no language models, no InceptionV1 examples, no architecture or tool comparison of interpretable share, no attribution graphs and no explanation-to-activation prediction scores. Its results concern the metric's behaviour, not any version's quantity. The depth trend (layer4 PSI above layer3) is related to V4's mention of messy late layers. However, it gives no share of interpretable neurons and no test of causes. Its appeal to superposition is interpretation, not a test.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is mostly right. Add that the authors interpret the depth trend as later layers packing concepts via superposition. They also say PSI rankings and D scores are sensitive to top-K and text-encoder choice (ρ≈0.21). The superposition reading is asserted, not tested.
record.recipe_differences: The paper introduces a null-calibrated PSI using CLIP patch embeddings, clustering, class-label alignment, and open-vocabulary text matching, then validates selected prototypes with patch swaps. It does not use the original Qwen3 pole-audit procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: PSI ranking stability varied with the number of top patches: the text reports correlation increasing from 0.41 at K = 30 toward the K = 50 baseline, while Appendix Figure 4 reports approximately 0.21 at K=10 and 0.42 at K=40. D scores across two CLIP text heads had Spearman's ρ ≈ 0.21.

fits_no_version.finding: In ResNet-50, layer4 PSI was higher than layer3 (median layer4 above layer3's 75th percentile; KS p ≪ 1e-6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under a CLIP-based clustering metric, later-layer CNN channels show more decomposable top-activation sets than mid-layer channels.

fits_no_version.finding: Channel 1721 fires on dog faces, with pose or viewpoint subclusters of low semantic distinctness. Channel 1680 splits about 54/46 into columns versus foliage.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some channels' top activations split into distinct clusters, while others hold one concept with pose subvariants. These are qualitative single examples only.

fits_no_version.finding: PSI separates real channels from the null, and aligned patch swaps on 10 high-PSI channels raise activation versus controls.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: PSI-discovered prototypes are causally relevant to the selected channels' activation. This is a validation of the method only.

record.problems: The layer4 PSI-versus-null AUROC is inconsistent: Table 1 reports 0.987, while Section 5.1 and Figure 2b report 0.599. The causal patch-swap analysis uses only 10 selected high-PSI layer4 neurons. Numerical results for several patch-swap controls are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the at-most-60-row limit. Method-sensitivity results on top-patch count, the alternative text encoder, and optimal cluster counts are summarized in gate_note and method_sensitivity rather than recorded as claim-version results.

untested.parts: All: shares in other LMs, dense or MoE, at any scale.
All: the InceptionV1 cat/car neuron and recursive generalization versus superposition. The paper only mentions cat faces/car fronts in its intro as an example of polysemanticity.
All: causes of messy late-layer neurons, and interpretable-share changes with tools or architectures in InceptionV1-sized models.
All: neuron-level attribution graphs without a replacement model.
All: whether activating-example explanations predict firing elsewhere.
All: simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The study is a vision-CNN metric paper with no share-of-interpretable-neurons figure, so it cannot be compared with V1, V2 or V4 numbers. The AUROC inconsistency (0.987 vs 0.599) and the small causal sample (10 selected neurons) weaken even its own claims. The high-PSI channel examples do not distinguish polysemanticity from a shared higher-level feature.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole shares and the proportions with one, two, or not-yet-understood jobs.
Language models, dense versus mixture-of-experts models, and scaling to trillions of parameters.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example and whether it reflects a coherent shared feature rather than superposition.
The causes of messy late-layer neurons, comparisons of architecture or tools, and the claimed interpretable-neuron share estimates for InceptionV1-sized models.
Attribution graphs, behavioral explanation using a model's own neurons, and reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict firing on separate examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.uncertainty: 95% CI shown in the figure; numerical interval not stated

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Compared PSI distributions between layer3 and layer4 channels.
rows.value: Layer4 distribution shifted higher; its median exceeded the 75th percentile of layer3; two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test p ≪ 10^-6
rows.note: The authors conclude that their PSI measure indicates greater polysemanticity in layer4 than layer3.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Swapped in an aligned patch from the same prototype cluster at the target neuron's peak-activating patch.
rows.value: Mean increase of +0.15 relative to the neuron's typical activation range
rows.uncertainty: Difference between aligned and all control conditions significant by paired t-tests, p < 0.05
rows.note: The paper states that aligned patch swaps consistently increased activation.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Swapped in a non-aligned patch from a different prototype cluster.
rows.value: Significant decrease in activation; no numerical change stated
rows.uncertainty: Aligned versus control condition difference, paired t-test p < 0.05
rows.note: The control did not produce the aligned condition's increase.
rows.check: The control produced a significant decrease in activation, not a weaker increase, so 'partial' misreads it. It is a method-validation control, not a claim result.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Swapped in a patch from an unrelated neuron.
rows.value: Significant decrease in activation; no numerical change stated
rows.uncertainty: Aligned versus control condition difference, paired t-test p < 0.05
rows.note: The control did not produce the aligned condition's increase.
rows.check: The random-patch control also produced a significant decrease, not a partial increase. It is a method-validation control.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Inserted an aligned patch at a different, randomly selected image location.
rows.measure: Change in activation at the original target site
rows.uncertainty: Aligned versus control condition difference, paired t-test p < 0.05
rows.note: The paper describes virtually no change at the original site.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Modified a different image region rather than the target patch location.
rows.value: Did not produce an increase similar to the aligned condition; numerical change not stated
rows.uncertainty: Aligned versus control condition difference, paired t-test p < 0.05
rows.note: The paper says this control ruled out generic image-modification effects.
rows.check: No direction or value is given for ablate-elsewhere beyond 'not a similar increase', so 'partial' cannot be read.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Examined the top activating patches for a high-PSI channel.
rows.value: Two visually distinct clusters, approximately 54/46; examples described as vertical/column-like structures and foliage/texture backgrounds
rows.note: A qualitative example of a channel the authors characterize as high-PSI and polysemantic.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Examined the top activating patches for a lower-PSI channel.
rows.measure: Qualitative coherence and semantic distinctness of top-activation patches
rows.value: Consistently responded to dog faces; minor pose/viewpoint subclusters were described as having low semantic distinctness and lower overall PSI
rows.note: The paper presents this as a more monosemantic comparison channel.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: It discusses polysemantic neurons in general and does not cite or test the essay's claim.

tranche.reason: The paper builds and validates a polysemanticity score (PSI) for ResNet-50 channels in layer3 and layer4. It reports no share of interpretable or one-job neurons, no InceptionV1 or language-model results, and no comparison of architectures or tools. Its layer4 > layer3 depth trend is put down to superposition, which it asserts but does not test.

source_check.notes: Both rows are single qualitative examples (Sec 5.4, Fig 3; layer4 of an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50, evaluated on Tiny-ImageNet). The text contradicts itself on the layer4 PSI AUROC: 0.599 in Sec 5.1 and Fig 2b, but 0.987 in Table 1 and about 0.99 in the intro. No statement here uses that number.
